steps.working: Angle ADB = 196 ÷ 2 = 98°, by the same theorem.
steps.decision: Check: 82 + 98 = 180. A, C, B and D make a cyclic quadrilateral, and its opposite angles always do.

text: How the paper asks: a reason every line

md: The answer lines read 'Angle ___ = ___° because ___'. Each line pays one mark for the angle and one for its reason, and the reason is paid only when its angle is right (November 2025, Q20(b)). Every paper from 2018 to 2026 sets one circle-theorem question, in the last third.

Four losses recur in the reports: a reason missing 'opposite' or 'cyclic' (November 2025); 'the angle is double', which names neither angle; 'isosceles' with nothing on why the sides are equal (November 2024); and opposite angles called equal (Summer 2025).

prompt: A diameter makes a straight angle, 180°, at the centre. Halving it gives which theorem?
options: The angle in a semicircle is 90°
Angles in the same segment are equal
The alternate segment theorem
answer: The angle in a semicircle is 90°
explain: The angle at the circumference on a diameter is half of the straight centre angle: 180 ÷ 2 = 90°. That is the angle in a semicircle, the centre theorem again, just as See it used the same theorem for the cyclic quadrilateral.

optionNotes.option: Angles in the same segment are equal
optionNotes.why: Same segment compares two angles on one chord; halving the straight angle is about a single angle, and it comes out as 90°.

optionNotes.option: The alternate segment theorem
optionNotes.why: The alternate segment theorem needs a tangent, and halving a straight centre angle uses none.

twin.answer: Angles in the same segment are equal
twin.explain: Both angles are half of the same centre angle, so they are equal: angles in the same segment are equal.

optionNotes.option: The angle in a semicircle is 90°
optionNotes.why: That needs the chord to be a diameter; here it is any chord, and the point is that the two angles match.

optionNotes.option: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°
optionNotes.why: Opposite angles sit on opposite arcs; these two are on the same arc, so they are equal, not a pair making 180°.
